questions.q: Roll one fair die, $\Omega = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$. What is $P(\text{Prime})$ for the event Prime $= \{2,3,5\}$?
questions.explain: $P(A) = |A|/|\Omega| = 3/6 = 1/2$. $2/3$ wrongly counts 1 as prime; $3/5$ divides by the wrong total — the denominator is always $|\Omega| = 6$.

questions.q: Rolling two dice, the sums $\{2, 3, \dots, 12\}$ are 11 possible results. What is $P(\text{sum} = 7)$?
questions.explain: The 11 sums are not equally likely. Count in the 36 equally likely ordered pairs: the diagonal $(1,6),(2,5),\dots,(6,1)$ has 6 pairs, so $6/36 = 1/6$. $1/11$ is the classic counting trap.

questions.q: With one die, let $A$ = Even $\{2,4,6\}$ and $B$ = Prime $\{2,3,5\}$. What is $P(A \cup B)$?
questions.explain: $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B| = 3 + 3 - 1 = 5$ (only 2 is in both), so $P = 5/6$. Answering $1$ forgets to subtract the double-counted overlap.
